title: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins

cards.explanation: This is a historical causation framework, not a requirement that every modern infectious disease fits all postulates. The slide illustrates isolation, comparison and reproduction of disease.
cards.text: Koch’s postulates link a suspected microorganism with the {{c1::disease it causes}}.
cards.question: Koch’s postulates link a suspected microorganism with the {{c1::disease it causes}}.

cards.explanation: The first illustrated step begins with an affected animal. The classical association is not an absolute modern rule excluding asymptomatic carriage.
cards.text: In the classical Koch framework, the suspected organism is associated with {{c1::diseased hosts}}.
cards.question: In the classical Koch framework, the suspected organism is associated with {{c1::diseased hosts}}.

cards.explanation: This is the historical evidence standard illustrated on the slide, rather than a claim that every pathogen grows independently in culture.
cards.text: The isolation stage of Koch’s framework seeks a {{c1::pure culture}} of the suspected organism.
cards.question: The isolation stage of Koch’s framework seeks a {{c1::pure culture}} of the suspected organism.

cards.explanation: This is a conceptual account of the historical postulates, not an instruction to perform an experiment.
cards.text: Reproduction of the same disease in a susceptible host supports a proposed {{c1::causal link}} in Koch’s framework.
cards.question: Reproduction of the same disease in a susceptible host supports a proposed {{c1::causal link}} in Koch’s framework.

cards.explanation: The diagram labels identical microorganisms recovered after disease is reproduced; identification closes the causal argument.
cards.text: The final Koch comparison requires the recovered microorganism to be {{c1::the same as the original organism}}.
cards.question: The final Koch comparison requires the recovered microorganism to be {{c1::the same as the original organism}}.
cards.answer: the same as the original organism

cards.explanation: The lecture organises these traits around attachment, colonisation, immune evasion and toxin-mediated damage.
cards.text: A bacterial trait that enhances its ability to cause disease is a {{c1::virulence factor}}.
cards.question: A bacterial trait that enhances its ability to cause disease is a {{c1::virulence factor}}.

cards.explanation: This helps establish infection before successful colonisation. It is distinct from subsequent growth in the host.
cards.text: Attachment to host cells or surfaces is called {{c1::adherence}}.
cards.question: Attachment to host cells or surfaces is called {{c1::adherence}}.

cards.explanation: Attachment alone does not establish that the organism can obtain the conditions and nutrients needed to grow.
cards.text: Surviving and multiplying in an appropriate host site constitutes {{c1::colonisation}}.
cards.question: Surviving and multiplying in an appropriate host site constitutes {{c1::colonisation}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture names this stage but does not explain specific capsule, complement or antibody-evasion mechanisms. Those mechanisms are not inferred from the heading.
cards.text: Avoiding or resisting host defences contributes to {{c1::immune evasion}}.
cards.question: Avoiding or resisting host defences contributes to {{c1::immune evasion}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s left-hand diagram labels adhesin and receptor; their molecular compatibility helps explain attachment to particular tissues.
cards.text: Specific bacterial adhesion involves a microbial ligand binding a complementary host {{c1::receptor}}.
cards.question: Specific bacterial adhesion involves a microbial ligand binding a complementary host {{c1::receptor}}.

cards.explanation: Adhesins bind host structures; the word does not mean the host receptor itself.
cards.text: A microbial surface ligand that mediates attachment is an {{c1::adhesin}}.
cards.question: A microbial surface ligand that mediates attachment is an {{c1::adhesin}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture highlights their adherence role; not every pilus has an identical function.
cards.text: The appendages named alongside adhesins as common attachment structures are {{c1::pili}}.
cards.question: The appendages named alongside adhesins as common attachment structures are {{c1::pili}}.

cards.explanation: This is the labelled example on the slide, not a species identification inferred from bacterial shape.
cards.text: The adhesion micrograph labels E. coli attached to human {{c1::bladder cells}}.
cards.question: The adhesion micrograph labels E. coli attached to human {{c1::bladder cells}}.

cards.explanation: This is the non-invasive toxin-producing route in the lecture. Its phrase “no intercellular penetration” should not be read as a precise account of every between-cell route.
cards.text: Bacteria can cause mucosal disease by adhering and producing toxin without {{c1::entering epithelial cells}}.
cards.question: Bacteria can cause mucosal disease by adhering and producing toxin without {{c1::entering epithelial cells}}.

cards.explanation: The slide distinguishes cell entry from adherence alone and from spread into deeper tissue.
cards.text: One mucosal route involves epithelial entry through {{c1::endocytosis}}.
cards.question: One mucosal route involves epithelial entry through {{c1::endocytosis}}.

cards.explanation: The third listed pattern is deeper invasion rather than remaining on or within the epithelium.
cards.text: Spread beyond the mucosal epithelium reaches the {{c1::submucosal layers}}.
cards.question: Spread beyond the mucosal epithelium reaches the {{c1::submucosal layers}}.

cards.explanation: The body is not a uniformly nutrient-rich environment for every bacterium.
cards.text: Successful colonisation requires suitable environmental conditions and adequate {{c1::nutrients}}.
cards.question: Successful colonisation requires suitable environmental conditions and adequate {{c1::nutrients}}.

cards.explanation: Much host iron is bound or stored rather than freely available.
cards.text: A trace element highlighted as difficult for bacteria to obtain in the host is {{c1::iron}}.
cards.question: A trace element highlighted as difficult for bacteria to obtain in the host is {{c1::iron}}.

cards.explanation: The slide also lists haem-associated iron. Its numerical iron concentrations and units are ambiguous, so these are not made into quantitative recall cards.
cards.text: Ferritin and haemosiderin are intracellular {{c1::iron stores}}.
cards.question: Ferritin and haemosiderin are intracellular {{c1::iron stores}}.

cards.explanation: Protein binding limits free iron availability to invading organisms.
cards.text: The extracellular iron-binding proteins named in the lecture are transferrin and {{c1::lactoferrin}}.
cards.question: The extracellular iron-binding proteins named in the lecture are transferrin and {{c1::lactoferrin}}.

cards.explanation: They help acquire iron in an environment where much of it is host-bound.
cards.text: High-affinity iron-binding molecules produced by bacteria are {{c1::siderophores}}.
cards.question: High-affinity iron-binding molecules produced by bacteria are {{c1::siderophores}}.

cards.explanation: This is distinct from secreting siderophores, although both address iron limitation.
cards.text: Some pathogens acquire host iron through specific receptors for {{c1::transferrin}}.
cards.question: Some pathogens acquire host iron through specific receptors for {{c1::transferrin}}.

cards.explanation: The slide lists haem acquisition alongside siderophores and transferrin receptors.
cards.text: Another bacterial iron source named in the lecture is liberated {{c1::haem}}.
cards.question: Another bacterial iron source named in the lecture is liberated {{c1::haem}}.

cards.explanation: A potent toxin can produce substantial damage even when bacterial numbers alone do not explain the clinical picture.
cards.text: Bacterial disease severity can depend on toxin activity rather than simply the {{c1::number of bacteria}}.
cards.question: Bacterial disease severity can depend on toxin activity rather than simply the {{c1::number of bacteria}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture emphasises the small intestine. This is a functional category, not the name of one molecular mechanism.
cards.text: A toxin targeting intestinal function is an {{c1::enterotoxin}}.
cards.question: A toxin targeting intestinal function is an {{c1::enterotoxin}}.

cards.explanation: The slide emphasises distant effects; this is not a requirement that every exotoxin must travel to a distant organ.
cards.text: An exotoxin can produce effects {{c1::away from the bacterial infection site}}.
cards.question: An exotoxin can produce effects {{c1::away from the bacterial infection site}}.
cards.answer: away from the bacterial infection site

cards.explanation: This supplies the definition requested by the slide’s “What are they?” prompt. Endotoxin is a distinct topic, deferred to another lecture.
cards.text: Exotoxins are bacterial {{c1::protein toxins}}.
cards.question: Exotoxins are bacterial {{c1::protein toxins}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture contrasts these organisms with examples dominated by a characteristic toxin.
cards.text: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes and Pseudomonas aeruginosa can produce {{c1::multiple different toxins}}.
cards.question: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes and Pseudomonas aeruginosa can produce {{c1::multiple different toxins}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s “single toxin” wording is a simplification, not a rule that each listed species can produce only one toxin or virulence factor.
cards.text: The characteristic toxin associated with Vibrio cholerae is {{c1::cholera toxin}}.
cards.question: The characteristic toxin associated with Vibrio cholerae is {{c1::cholera toxin}}.

cards.explanation: The slides repeat this point on pages 27 and 38. Their request for a named plasmid example is left blank; no unsupported example is supplied.
cards.text: Some bacterial toxin genes are carried on plasmids or {{c1::bacteriophages}}.
cards.question: Some bacterial toxin genes are carried on plasmids or {{c1::bacteriophages}}.

cards.explanation: Botulinum and tetanus toxins are the named examples.
cards.text: A toxin acting on the nervous system is a {{c1::neurotoxin}}.
cards.question: A toxin acting on the nervous system is a {{c1::neurotoxin}}.

cards.explanation: The source reports subsequent breathing/swallowing difficulty and cardiac problems. The case history supports a principle, not a universal timetable for every patient.
cards.text: The diphtheria case illustrates that improvement in throat symptoms does not exclude later {{c1::systemic complications}}.
cards.question: The diphtheria case illustrates that improvement in throat symptoms does not exclude later {{c1::systemic complications}}.

cards.explanation: Toxigenicity depends on possession and expression of the toxin gene, not simply the species name.
cards.text: The bacterium producing diphtheria toxin is {{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}.
cards.question: The bacterium producing diphtheria toxin is {{c1::Corynebacterium diphtheriae}}.

cards.explanation: This is the lecture’s concrete example of a phage-encoded toxin.
cards.text: The diphtheria toxin gene is carried by a {{c1::β bacteriophage}}.
cards.question: The diphtheria toxin gene is carried by a {{c1::β bacteriophage}}.

cards.explanation: This is the labelled clinical image. The case illustrates upper-airway illness with potentially serious systemic effects; it is not a stand-alone diagnostic rule.
cards.text: The grey adherent coating illustrated over the tonsils in diphtheria is a {{c1::pseudomembrane}}.
cards.question: The grey adherent coating illustrated over the tonsils in diphtheria is a {{c1::pseudomembrane}}.

cards.explanation: The AB organisation separates enzymatic activity from binding and entry functions.
cards.text: The catalytic component of diphtheria toxin is fragment {{c1::A}}.
cards.question: The catalytic component of diphtheria toxin is fragment {{c1::A}}.

cards.explanation: Fragment A carries the catalytic activity; B enables delivery to the target cell.
cards.text: Diphtheria toxin fragment B mediates host-cell {{c1::binding and entry}}.
cards.question: Diphtheria toxin fragment B mediates host-cell {{c1::binding and entry}}.

cards.explanation: The next slide’s mechanism image shows receptor binding followed by vesicle/endosome uptake.
cards.text: Diphtheria toxin enters a host cell by {{c1::endocytosis}}.
cards.question: Diphtheria toxin enters a host cell by {{c1::endocytosis}}.

cards.explanation: The figure labels EF-2 at the final reaction. Its modification prevents protein synthesis.
cards.text: The host translation factor targeted by diphtheria toxin is {{c1::EF-2}}.
cards.question: The host translation factor targeted by diphtheria toxin is {{c1::EF-2}}.

cards.explanation: The figure shows NAD donating the ADP-ribose group and nicotinamide being released.
cards.text: Diphtheria toxin inhibits translation by {{c1::ADP-ribosylating EF-2}}.
cards.question: Diphtheria toxin inhibits translation by {{c1::ADP-ribosylating EF-2}}.

cards.explanation: The effect follows inactivation of EF-2 rather than direct inhibition of adenylate cyclase.
cards.text: The immediate biosynthetic process inhibited by diphtheria toxin is {{c1::protein synthesis}}.
cards.question: The immediate biosynthetic process inhibited by diphtheria toxin is {{c1::protein synthesis}}.

cards.explanation: The slide gives the co-repressor relationship; with sufficient iron, iron-dependent repression reduces toxin gene expression. This is regulation of toxin production, not a treatment instruction.
cards.text: Iron acts as a {{c1::co-repressor}} of diphtheria toxin production.
cards.question: Iron acts as a {{c1::co-repressor}} of diphtheria toxin production.

cards.explanation: The source describes double vision, swallowing difficulty and ventilation. Food history plus symptoms require appropriate investigation, not diagnosis from one symptom alone.
cards.text: The cheese-associated botulism case illustrates severe weakness progressing to {{c1::respiratory failure}}.
cards.question: The cheese-associated botulism case illustrates severe weakness progressing to {{c1::respiratory failure}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture’s food-associated case concerns ingestion of preformed neurotoxin; this is not a description of every form of botulism.
cards.text: The principal organism named for botulinum toxin is {{c1::Clostridium botulinum}}.
cards.question: The principal organism named for botulinum toxin is {{c1::Clostridium botulinum}}.

cards.explanation: Distinguish toxin-mediated foodborne disease from assuming bacterial invasion is needed at the neuromuscular target.
cards.text: The foodborne botulism example follows ingestion of {{c1::preformed neurotoxin}}.
cards.question: The foodborne botulism example follows ingestion of {{c1::preformed neurotoxin}}.

cards.explanation: This is the lecture’s teaching list; its “6/7 toxins” statement is not used as an exhaustive modern classification.
cards.text: The classical human-associated botulinum toxin types listed are A, B, E and {{c1::F}}.
cards.question: The classical human-associated botulinum toxin types listed are A, B, E and {{c1::F}}.

cards.explanation: The slide’s phrase “disulphide chain” means a bond linking the two polypeptide chains.
cards.text: Botulinum toxin contains a light chain and a heavy chain joined by a {{c1::disulphide bond}}.
cards.question: Botulinum toxin contains a light chain and a heavy chain joined by a {{c1::disulphide bond}}.

cards.explanation: The structural image contrasts this with the heavy chain’s binding/delivery roles.
cards.text: Botulinum toxin’s enzymatic activity resides in its {{c1::light chain}}.
cards.question: Botulinum toxin’s enzymatic activity resides in its {{c1::light chain}}.

cards.explanation: The two chains have complementary functions; the heavy chain is not the catalytic protease.
cards.text: Botulinum toxin’s heavy chain contributes to neuronal {{c1::binding and delivery}}.
cards.question: Botulinum toxin’s heavy chain contributes to neuronal {{c1::binding and delivery}}.

cards.explanation: The image places the toxin on the transmitter-releasing side, not the muscle receptor.
cards.text: The relevant botulinum toxin target is the {{c1::presynaptic nerve terminal}} at the neuromuscular junction.
cards.question: The relevant botulinum toxin target is the {{c1::presynaptic nerve terminal}} at the neuromuscular junction.

cards.explanation: The labelled diagram links these proteins with vesicle fusion and transmitter release; it does not specify that every toxin type cleaves the same SNARE.
cards.text: Botulinum toxin light chain cleaves {{c1::SNARE proteins}}.
cards.question: Botulinum toxin light chain cleaves {{c1::SNARE proteins}}.

cards.explanation: Vesicles fail to release transmitter normally; this is not direct blockade of acetylcholine binding to its muscle receptor.
cards.text: Cleavage of presynaptic SNARE proteins reduces {{c1::acetylcholine release}}.
cards.question: Cleavage of presynaptic SNARE proteins reduces {{c1::acetylcholine release}}.

cards.explanation: This explains weakness and the potential for respiratory failure in the case. The source diagram supports the presynaptic mechanism.
cards.text: Reduced acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction impairs {{c1::muscle contraction}}.
cards.question: Reduced acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction impairs {{c1::muscle contraction}}.

cards.explanation: This is a case association, not a claim that jaw pain alone diagnoses tetanus.
cards.text: Jaw pain in a patient with incomplete vaccination is the clinical clue in the lecture’s {{c1::tetanus}} case.
cards.question: Jaw pain in a patient with incomplete vaccination is the clinical clue in the lecture’s {{c1::tetanus}} case.

cards.explanation: The case links suspected tetanus with jaw pain and incomplete vaccination.
cards.text: The organism associated with tetanus toxin is {{c1::Clostridium tetani}}.
cards.question: The organism associated with tetanus toxin is {{c1::Clostridium tetani}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture associates subsequent germination with oxygen-poor tissue.
cards.text: The tetanus entry route highlighted is a {{c1::break in the skin}}.
cards.question: The tetanus entry route highlighted is a {{c1::break in the skin}}.

cards.explanation: The slide calls the tissue anoxic. Major local destruction is not required to explain toxin-mediated distant effects.
cards.text: C. tetani germination is favoured by {{c1::anaerobic tissue conditions}}.
cards.question: C. tetani germination is favoured by {{c1::anaerobic tissue conditions}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with the peripheral neuromuscular-junction mechanism illustrated for botulinum toxin. The slides do not show the detailed inhibitory-neuron pathway.
cards.text: The nervous-system site emphasised for tetanus toxin is the {{c1::central nervous system}}.
cards.question: The nervous-system site emphasised for tetanus toxin is the {{c1::central nervous system}}.

cards.explanation: Structural resemblance does not establish identical target sites or clinical effects.
cards.text: Tetanus toxin has a two-polypeptide structure similar to, but {{c1::not identical to}}, botulinum toxin.
cards.question: Tetanus toxin has a two-polypeptide structure similar to, but {{c1::not identical to}}, botulinum toxin.

cards.explanation: The organism’s intestinal toxin action is developed in the following slides.
cards.text: Cholera is a toxin-mediated disease caused by {{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}.
cards.question: Cholera is a toxin-mediated disease caused by {{c1::Vibrio cholerae}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture uses drinking water as an example; it does not establish that every container shown is contaminated.
cards.text: The transmission route highlighted for cholera is {{c1::faecal–oral}} spread through contaminated water.
cards.question: The transmission route highlighted for cholera is {{c1::faecal–oral}} spread through contaminated water.

cards.explanation: The main danger highlighted is severe dehydration, rather than direct bacterial invasion of distant tissues.
cards.text: Profuse cholera diarrhoea can rapidly cause water loss and {{c1::electrolyte depletion}}.
cards.question: Profuse cholera diarrhoea can rapidly cause water loss and {{c1::electrolyte depletion}}.

cards.explanation: The appearance is descriptive, not sufficient alone to identify the pathogen.
cards.text: The stool appearance described in severe cholera is {{c1::rice-water stool}}.
cards.question: The stool appearance described in severe cholera is {{c1::rice-water stool}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture illustrates why sanitation matters. Its numerical shedding estimates are not treated as fixed values for every patient.
cards.text: Heavy shedding of vibrios in diarrhoeal stool can increase {{c1::environmental contamination}}.
cards.question: Heavy shedding of vibrios in diarrhoeal stool can increase {{c1::environmental contamination}}.

cards.explanation: This is the AB₅ organisation: B forms a binding ring around the A-associated structure.
cards.text: Cholera toxin has one A subunit and {{c1::five B subunits}}.
cards.question: Cholera toxin has one A subunit and {{c1::five B subunits}}.

cards.explanation: The source divides A into A1 and A2; A1 performs the ADP-ribosylation reaction described later.
cards.text: Cholera toxin’s enzymatically active A fragment is {{c1::A1}}.
cards.question: Cholera toxin’s enzymatically active A fragment is {{c1::A1}}.

cards.explanation: This distinguishes receptor recognition from A1’s catalytic activity.
cards.text: The five B subunits of cholera toxin primarily mediate {{c1::binding to the host cell}}.
cards.question: The five B subunits of cholera toxin primarily mediate {{c1::binding to the host cell}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture diagram contrasts an active GTP-associated state with an inactive state after hydrolysis.
cards.text: The GTP-bound Gαs state promotes {{c1::adenylate cyclase activity}}.
cards.question: The GTP-bound Gαs state promotes {{c1::adenylate cyclase activity}}.

cards.explanation: This provides the off-switch that cholera toxin disrupts. The older drawing labels an arrow Gi; do not infer that cholera toxin directly targets Gi.
cards.text: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP normally helps {{c1::switch off Gαs signalling}}.
cards.question: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP normally helps {{c1::switch off Gαs signalling}}.

cards.explanation: Binding provides the receptor-level specificity illustrated in the mechanism diagram.
cards.text: Cholera toxin B binds the host-cell ganglioside {{c1::GM1}}.
cards.question: Cholera toxin B binds the host-cell ganglioside {{c1::GM1}}.

cards.explanation: This is the stimulatory G-protein α subunit associated with adenylate cyclase; the slide’s “Gas” notation refers to Gαs.
cards.text: The regulatory protein targeted by cholera toxin A1 is {{c1::Gαs}}.
cards.question: The regulatory protein targeted by cholera toxin A1 is {{c1::Gαs}}.

cards.explanation: A1 transfers the group to Gαs; the diagram also shows nicotinamide release.
cards.text: The donor of the ADP-ribose group in cholera toxin action is {{c1::NAD}}.
cards.question: The donor of the ADP-ribose group in cholera toxin action is {{c1::NAD}}.

cards.explanation: Diphtheria toxin also ADP-ribosylates a protein, but its target is EF-2 rather than Gαs.
cards.text: The chemical modification of Gαs by cholera toxin is {{c1::ADP-ribosylation}}.
cards.question: The chemical modification of Gαs by cholera toxin is {{c1::ADP-ribosylation}}.

cards.explanation: The key consequence is impaired GTPase-dependent inactivation of Gαs, not direct covalent modification of adenylate cyclase itself.
cards.text: ADP-ribosylated Gαs remains functionally {{c1::active}}.
cards.question: ADP-ribosylated Gαs remains functionally {{c1::active}}.

cards.explanation: This follows activation of the Gαs pathway.
cards.text: Persistent stimulation of adenylate cyclase raises intracellular {{c1::cAMP}}.
cards.question: Persistent stimulation of adenylate cyclase raises intracellular {{c1::cAMP}}.

cards.explanation: This explains secretory watery diarrhoea without requiring invasive destruction of intestinal cells.
cards.text: Raised cAMP changes intestinal ion transport, driving water and electrolytes {{c1::into the gut lumen}}.
cards.question: Raised cAMP changes intestinal ion transport, driving water and electrolytes {{c1::into the gut lumen}}.

cards.explanation: The source figure is a simplified older entry diagram, not a complete intracellular trafficking map. It is not used to invent a detailed route through organelles.
cards.text: In the toxin pathway, A1 reaches the cell interior while the B components serve the {{c1::binding function}}.
cards.question: In the toxin pathway, A1 reaches the cell interior while the B components serve the {{c1::binding function}}.

cards.explanation: It is associated with watery traveller’s diarrhoea and is cholera-like. The slide incorrectly conflates this with Shiga-like toxin; they are different toxin families.
cards.text: The E. coli toxin abbreviated LT means {{c1::heat-labile toxin}}.
cards.question: The E. coli toxin abbreviated LT means {{c1::heat-labile toxin}}.

cards.explanation: Correction to pages 39/42: Shiga-like toxins damage 28S rRNA rather than sharing cholera toxin’s GM1–Gαs–cAMP mechanism. The source also generalises Salmonella incorrectly; do not memorise it as a universal Shiga-toxin producer.
cards.text: E. coli LT is cholera-like, whereas Shiga-like toxin acts on {{c1::protein synthesis at the ribosome}}.
cards.question: E. coli LT is cholera-like, whereas Shiga-like toxin acts on {{c1::protein synthesis at the ribosome}}.

cards.explanation: This contrasts with the LT abbreviation for heat-labile E. coli toxin; heat stability is a toxin property, not proof that every contaminated food has the same risk.
cards.text: Staphylococcal enterotoxins are relatively {{c1::heat stable}}.
cards.question: Staphylococcal enterotoxins are relatively {{c1::heat stable}}.

cards.explanation: The slide names A–D as examples, not a complete modern catalogue of all staphylococcal enterotoxins.
cards.text: The staphylococcal enterotoxin highlighted as common in the lecture is {{c1::enterotoxin A}}.
cards.question: The staphylococcal enterotoxin highlighted as common in the lecture is {{c1::enterotoxin A}}.

cards.explanation: The lecture states stimulation of nerves in the gut. This functional link explains an enterotoxin effect without treating it as the same Gαs mechanism as cholera.
cards.text: Staphylococcal enterotoxin can stimulate gut neural pathways associated with {{c1::vomiting}}.
cards.question: Staphylococcal enterotoxin can stimulate gut neural pathways associated with {{c1::vomiting}}.

should

factor play in illness.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 5
slides.text:
Stages of microbiological 
pathogenicity
• Pathogenicity/Virulence factors influence the 
bacterial ability to survive upon entering the 
host: 
Adherence to cells and surface
Be able to colonise in the host
Evasion of the immune system
Destroy tissue through exotoxin production.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 6
slides.text:
Adherence
• Most infection begin on mucus membrane
• First bacteria must attach to host:
– Nonspecific/specific
• Specific adherence occur between structures on the 
microbe and the hot cell
• Two common element include: Pili and adhesin

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 7
slides.text:
Microbial attacks on mucus 
membrane
• The are three possibilities:
1.
Adhere, production of exotoxin (but no 
intercellular penetration)
2.
Adhere, penetrate into mucosal epithelium via 
endocytosis
3.
Adhere, penetrate into mucosal epithelium  and 
into the sub mucosal layers.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 8
slides.text:
Colonisation
• To colonise and grow the bacteria must find 
appropriate nutrient and environment al 
conditions.
• Nutrients within the body are not always 
plentiful
– Soluble nutrient
– Trace elements also in short supply (iron).

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 9
slides.text:
How iron is stored in the body
• Bacteria require 0.4-40 µM of iron/day.
• Dietary intake of iron is ~10 mg/day:
– 10-18 µM free iron in plasma.
– 20 µM bound in plasma.
• Insoluble at pH 7.0 so bound to protein
– Intracellular; Ferritin, haemosidern and 
heam 
– Extracellular; Lactoferrin and transferrin

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 10
slides.text:
How bacteria obtain Iron
• Pathogens can acquire Iron from the 
host using a number of process:
– Production of siderophore
• High binding affinity for iron.
– Possess specific receptor for transferrin
– Acquire iron from liberated heam.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 11
slides.text:
Toxin
• In many cases disease caused by bacteria are 
not a result of the number of bacteria but 
due to the production of toxin.
• There are two classes of toxin
– Exotoxin –travel from focus of infection site to 
distant part of the body 
• Entertoxin-act on small intestine.
– Endotoxin (covered with Prof. M. Fielder)

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 12
slides.text:
Exotoxins.

• Bacteria that produc produce large variety 
of toxins include: Staphylococcus aureus, 
Streptococcus pyogenes & Pseudomonas 
aeruginosa

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 16
slides.text:
Case study 1 – Diphtheria 
• 9- year old boy, was diagnosed with 
pharyngitis, 3rd day his fever declined 
and sore throat resolved. (Washington 
et al., 2014)
• On day 5 he was taken to hospital with a 
number of symptoms  - inc. dyspnoea 
and dysphagia
• Patient when on to develop cardiac issue 
and later died

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 28
slides.text:
What is Cholera?
• The disease is caused by the production of a toxin 
by Vibrio cholerae.
• First described in Jessore, India in 1817
• Transmitted through the faecal-oral route via 
contaminated drinking water. 
• Symptoms
–   75% of those infected will not develop symptoms.
– Abrupt onset of diarrhoea leading to the  rapid loss electrolyte 
and dehydration – the main killer in this disease.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 29
slides.text:
Other characteristics
• The stool of an actively purging , severely 
ill cholera patient can resemble rice 
water.
• Stool can contain  108 viable vibrios per 
ml, such a patient could shed 2x1012 
cholera vibrios per day into the 
environment.

slides.topic: Virulence Factors — Adhesion, Iron Acquisition & Exotoxins — page 30
slides.text:
Structure of Cholera Toxin (CT)
• CT consists of two subunits and is a an example of 
an  A:B5 toxin.
• A subunit consists of two fractions
– A1
– A2
• The B subunit 
• The subunit A sits within the ring form by the B 
subunit.

How does the A unit enter the 
cell and what does it do

ganglioside GM1

cleaves  releasing the A1 peptide.
• The A1 fraction target is guanosine 5'-
triphosphate (GTP)-binding regulatory 
protein associated with membrane-bound 
adenylate cyclase (Gas).

cell and what does it do…….
• A1 enzymatically transfers ADP-ribose 
from nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide 
(NAD) to a target Gas resulting in ADP-
ribosylated of the protein.

What are the Consequences of 
Gas ADP ribosylation.
• The ADP-ribosylation reaction essentially 
locks adenylate cyclase in its "on mode”
• Increase cAMP levels change the flux of 
sodium/chloride across the cell membrane, 
resulting in the massive outflow of water 
and electrolytes. 
(Baron S, Medical Microbiology)

Other enterotoxins
• Escherichia coli and Salmonella sp can 
produce a shiga like toxin.
– Similar, structure, binding site mode of 
action to CT, however the toxin is not as 
potent.
• E. coli (LT) implicated in traveller’s 
diarrhoea
– Seen as watery diarrhoea.

Other enterotoxins #2
• Staphylococcal enterotoxin
• Mediated but a number of toxins; A-D, 
however toxin A is most ubiquitous.
• Single protein chain between 30-37.5KDa
– Heat stable.
• Toxin stimulate nerve in gut

Summary
• Virulence factor enhance bacteria 
ability to cause illness.
• Bacteria must:
–  adhere to host cell, 
– be able to colonise, 
– evaded the immune system 
– produce exotoxins.
